paragraphs: When experiments run in parallel, a fixed budget must cover both exploring different conditions and repeating measurements. Repetition is especially valuable when observations are noisy, but spending more on repeats leaves fewer opportunities to explore. This paper addresses that allocation problem when the amount of noise varies across experimental conditions.

The proposed BTS-RED framework contains three algorithms built around batch Thompson sampling. Two handle known and unknown noise variance, respectively. They adapt the number of repetitions to the condition being evaluated, assigning more repeats to noisier inputs. This makes replication part of the optimization decision instead of fixing the same repetition count for every condition.

A third algorithm addresses risk-averse preferences by considering both average performance and variability. The authors establish asymptotic no-regret guarantees for all three algorithms, including the settings with unequal noise levels. These are long-run guarantees rather than promises about each batch. Applications in precision agriculture and automated machine learning demonstrate the framework’s practical effectiveness.
neurips-2023-batch-bayesian-optimization.tldr: BTS-RED adaptively balances exploring experimental conditions and repeating noisy measurements, with variants for unknown noise and risk-averse objectives.

paragraphs: Causal discovery often uses conditional independence tests to determine which causal relationships could explain observed data. With independent, identically distributed observations, however, these tests generally leave multiple causal structures indistinguishable, even with unlimited data. This paper studies whether a different data structure can reveal distinctions that this usual setting cannot.

The authors consider exchangeable data and show how its richer conditional independence relationships can support causal discovery. Their causal de Finetti theorems establish that exchangeable distributions satisfying certain nontrivial conditional independences admit a representation through independent causal mechanisms. The conditional independence requirements matter: the result does not say that exchangeability alone identifies a causal structure.

The main identification theorem then shows that data generated by such an independent causal mechanism process allow its unique causal structure to be recovered through conditional independence tests. The authors turn this result into a discovery algorithm and demonstrate its applicability to data from multiple environments. The contribution connects structured variation across observations to stronger causal identification under the stated generative framework.
neurips-2023-causal-de-finetti-on-the-id.tldr: Under an independent causal mechanism framework, conditional independence relationships in exchangeable data can uniquely identify causal structure.

paragraphs: Sharing components across reinforcement learning tasks can help agents reuse useful behavior, but it can also create conflicts that hurt performance. Modular approaches try to manage this by assigning different functions to different components. This paper argues that combining those components only at the whole-task level misses conflicts that can arise within a task.

The proposed Contrastive Modules with Temporal Attention method addresses two sources of difficulty. Contrastive learning encourages modules to differ, reducing the tendency for multiple components to learn similar functions. Temporal attention combines shared modules at a finer level than a single combination for an entire task. Together, these choices aim to make sharing more selective while retaining distinct capabilities.

Experiments use Meta-World, a benchmark of robotic manipulation tasks. The authors report substantial improvements over the compared baselines and performance exceeding separate training on each task, which they describe as a first. These findings support the usefulness of both module diversity and finer-grained combination in the evaluated multi-task setting.
neurips-2023-contrastive-modules-with-te.tldr: CMTA combines distinct learned modules through temporal attention to reduce conflicts in multi-task reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must choose actions using an existing dataset rather than collecting new interactions. This paper asks how to learn a good policy when an adversary can corrupt samples throughout that dataset. Performance is measured against the optimal policy for the underlying uncorrupted decision process, so the goal is resilience to corrupted evidence.

The authors adapt uncertainty weighting to the offline setting. They introduce an iterative procedure that efficiently computes weights for batched samples and use it in a corruption-robust learning algorithm with general function approximation. Their guarantee assumes single-policy coverage and knowledge of the total corruption amount. The resulting extra error depends on corruption, dataset coverage, the function class, and the number of episodes.

For linear decision processes, the corruption-dependent contribution simplifies to order ζd/n, where ζ measures total corruption, d is the feature dimension, and n is the episode count. This matches an existing lower bound for that contribution. The match supports tightness of the corruption analysis in the linear setting, rather than establishing optimality of every part of the overall error bound.
neurips-2023-corruption-robust-offline-r.tldr: An uncertainty-weighted offline RL algorithm bounds the harm from corrupted data and matches the corruption-dependent lower bound for linear decision processes.

paragraphs: Chain-of-thought prompting asks language models to expose intermediate reasoning, but those extra steps can also introduce unsupported statements and propagate mistakes. Checking an entire argument at once is difficult even for advanced models. This paper instead treats verification as a sequence of smaller reasoning tasks tied to individual steps.

The authors introduce Natural Program, a natural-language format for deductive reasoning. It supports generating steps grounded in earlier statements and then verifying those steps using only the context and premises they need. Restricting each verification task this way makes the dependency between a conclusion and its supporting information explicit, rather than asking the model to assess a whole reasoning chain at once.

Verification is integrated throughout the deductive process. The authors report that this improves the rigor and trustworthiness of intermediate reasoning and also improves final-answer correctness on complex reasoning tasks. The stated result is an improvement in model reasoning and self-checking; the format uses natural language and does not itself establish that every generated argument is correct.
neurips-2023-deductive-verification-of-c.tldr: Natural Program structures reasoning into explicit steps that language models can verify individually, improving reasoning quality and answer correctness.

paragraphs: Text-to-SQL requires translating a natural-language request into a database query. The paper starts from a performance gap between prompting large language models and models trained specifically for this task. It investigates whether organizing the reasoning process more carefully can improve results obtained through in-context learning.

The central approach breaks query generation into smaller subproblems and feeds their solutions back into the language model. This gives later generation stages intermediate results to work from. Across experiments with three language models, the authors report improvements of roughly 10% over simple few-shot prompting, with performance approaching or exceeding the leading results in their comparisons.

On Spider’s held-out test set, execution accuracy reaches 85.3, compared with the previous leading result of 79.9 cited by the authors. The approach also beats many heavily fine-tuned models by at least 5% and reaches 55.9% execution accuracy on BIRD’s held-out test set. Both benchmark records are claims made at the time of the paper. The findings show that decomposition can make prompting substantially more competitive for database query generation.
neurips-2023-din-sql-decomposed-in-conte.tldr: DIN-SQL improves prompted text-to-SQL generation by solving smaller subproblems and supplying their results to the language model.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference software needs checks that its computed results are calibrated. A common approach uses simulation-based calibration with rank tests. The authors identify several difficulties with this approach: the choice of statistic is somewhat ad hoc, interactions are hard to examine, multiple tests complicate assessment, and a p-value does not measure the size of miscalibration.

Their alternative uses a flexible classifier to learn test statistics from data. Classification accuracy is converted into an interpretable divergence measure, giving a measure of discrepancy rather than only a significance assessment. The authors report that this approach typically has greater statistical power than the rank-based calibration test, meaning it can more effectively detect miscalibration in the settings considered.

The method accommodates different data-generating processes and can check simulation-based inference as well as methods such as Markov chain Monte Carlo and variational inference. An automated implementation combines neural networks with statistically motivated features. Numerical and real-data experiments validate the approach, supporting classification as a flexible tool for evaluating Bayesian computations.
neurips-2023-discriminative-calibration-.tldr: Discriminative calibration uses learned classifiers to check Bayesian computations and quantify miscalibration through an interpretable divergence measure.

paragraphs: Neural network policies can solve sequential decision problems, but their complexity makes them difficult to inspect and deploy with limited computation. Compact symbolic expressions offer a simpler policy representation. This paper addresses the training burden of earlier symbolic approaches, which often rely on complicated procedures and previously trained neural policies.

Efficient Symbolic Policy Learning learns a symbolic policy from scratch using gradients in an end-to-end procedure. A symbolic network defines the space of possible expressions, while a path selector identifies a compact policy within that space. Representing the selected policy through a differentiable expression enables gradient-based optimization. Off-policy training further improves learning efficiency.

The authors also extend the method to meta-reinforcement learning, where it generates symbolic policies for unseen tasks. Experiments show improved policy performance and substantially better data efficiency in single-task learning. In the meta-learning setting, the symbolic policies outperform the compared neural policies in performance and efficiency and show potential for interpretability. Thus, the contribution combines a simpler policy representation with a more direct way to learn it.
neurips-2023-efficient-symbolic-policy-l.tldr: ESPL learns compact symbolic policies directly with gradients, improving performance and efficiency in single-task and meta-reinforcement learning experiments.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning spreads model training across communicating nodes, making the pattern of communication part of the learning algorithm. Epidemic Learning changes that pattern repeatedly: in each round, every node sends its model updates to a random sample of s other nodes from a system of n nodes.

The authors analyze how this randomized, changing topology affects convergence. For smooth nonconvex losses, they bound the transient period before asymptotic linear speedup is reached by O(n³/s²) iterations. Compared with the cited best-known O(n³) bound, this improves the bound by a factor of s². The result links the number of randomly selected communication partners to how quickly the algorithm reaches its favorable long-run regime.

An empirical evaluation uses a network of 96 nodes. Epidemic Learning converges up to 1.7 times faster than the compared decentralized algorithms and achieves 2.2% higher accuracy for the same communication volume. These findings complement the analysis by showing that randomized communication can improve practical training progress as well as theoretical convergence properties.
neurips-2023-epidemic-learning-boosting-.tldr: Epidemic Learning randomly changes communication partners each round to improve decentralized training convergence and communication efficiency.

paragraphs: LIME explains a black-box prediction by approximating model behavior near an input, but its explanations can change with random seeds and poorly reflect nearby behavior. This paper traces these problems to specific parts of the method. Small sample weights allow regularization to dominate and slow convergence, while its sampling is nonlocal and biased toward a reference.

The authors propose GLIME, a framework that extends LIME and incorporates several earlier methods. Within it, they derive an equivalent formulation of LIME that converges substantially faster and improves stability. This addresses the numerical and weighting issues underlying explanation variability without treating instability as merely an unavoidable consequence of random sampling.

GLIME also uses a local, unbiased sampling distribution to improve fidelity to the model’s behavior near the input. With this choice, explanations no longer depend on the reference selection. The framework allows users to choose sampling distributions for different scenarios. Its contribution therefore joins an explanation of LIME’s failure modes with concrete changes to convergence and neighborhood sampling.
neurips-2023-glime-general-stable-and-lo.tldr: GLIME improves LIME’s stability and local fidelity by addressing sample weighting and using local, unbiased sampling.

paragraphs: Dictionary learning seeks a set of basic components and sparse coefficients that together represent observed data. This paper proposes recovering them by minimizing the dictionary matrix’s determinant, interpreted as its volume, while requiring every row of the coefficient matrix to have unit ℓ1 norm. The formulation is designed to support a global recovery guarantee.

The guarantee holds under a geometric condition on vectors derived from the coefficients: they lie within an ℓ∞ ball, while their convex hull contains an ℓ2 ball. Under this condition, every global optimum recovers the true factors up to permutation and scaling. The dictionary itself needs only to be nonsingular, without an additional requirement that its components be mutually incoherent.

For coefficients generated by a Bernoulli-Gaussian model, the authors show global identifiability with overwhelming probability once the sample count exceeds a constant times k log k, where k is the number of dictionary components. They also develop optimization algorithms, including efficient linearized-ADMM updates. Numerical experiments demonstrate effective recovery, complementing the theorem about global optima.
neurips-2023-global-identifiability-of-e.tldr: A volume-minimizing dictionary learning formulation guarantees global recovery under stated coefficient conditions and only nonsingularity of the dictionary.

paragraphs: Molecular dynamics faces a large separation between the tiny steps needed for stable simulation and the long times over which important molecular behavior unfolds. The abstract contrasts integration steps around 10⁻¹⁵ seconds with processes that may require sampling over 10⁻¹ seconds. Repeating these simulations independently for each molecular system adds to the computational challenge.

Implicit Transfer Operator Learning trains surrogate models of the simulation process at multiple time resolutions. The implementation combines denoising diffusion probabilistic models with a new SE(3)-equivariant architecture, respecting spatial rotations and translations. The authors show that the resulting models generate self-consistent stochastic dynamics across multiple timescales, including settings where only part of the system is observed.

They also introduce a coarse-grained model that quantitatively models all-atom molecular dynamics using coarse molecular representations. This connects flexibility in time resolution with flexibility in spatial detail. The work is presented as a step toward accelerating molecular dynamics across both dimensions, with the reported findings centered on learned dynamics and their consistency.
neurips-2023-implicit-transfer-operator-.tldr: Implicit Transfer Operator Learning models molecular dynamics across multiple timescales and supports coarse representations of all-atom behavior.

paragraphs: An AI agent interacting with people can change their actions and their underlying strategies. This paper studies how to use that influence when people perform suboptimally, for example because of limited information or cognitive biases. Assuming that human behavior is already nearly optimal would miss the very behavior the agent needs to improve.

The authors learn from an offline dataset of human-human interactions. This avoids relying on potentially unsafe online experimentation with people or an impractical high-fidelity simulator. Their central observation is that offline reinforcement learning can extend and combine elements of observed behavior to learn effective influence, even when the dataset contains no examples of successful influence.

The demonstrations address two challenges. First, agents trained on suboptimal interactions across several tasks learn strategies that guide people toward better performance, including on new tasks. Second, modeling and conditioning on human behavior lets agents influence underlying human strategies as well as immediate actions, and adapt when those strategies change. The findings show a route from imperfect interaction data to improved collaboration.
neurips-2023-learning-to-influence-human.tldr: Offline reinforcement learning can combine imperfect human interaction data into strategies that improve human performance and adapt to changing behavior.

paragraphs: Reducing the number of parameters updated during fine-tuning lowers optimizer memory, but storing a large language model’s pretrained weights remains expensive. Quantization reduces weight storage, yet many quantization methods focus on deployment. This paper connects these two approaches so that a model can remain compressed while being adapted to a task.

Parameter-Efficient and Quantization-aware Adaptation, or PEQA, updates only the quantization scales. It applies directly to quantized models, reducing optimizer-state overhead while retaining the smaller model representation. The quantization structure remains intact after fine-tuning, which allows the adapted model to retain the inference advantages of its compressed form.

The authors apply PEQA to models with up to 65 billion parameters and use instruction data to assess reasoning and comprehension after adaptation. Their results show that models quantized below four-bit precision can recover, or sometimes improve on, their original full-precision performance in language modeling, few-shot in-context learning, and comprehension. This is evidence that adjusting quantization scales can provide useful adaptation despite the restricted set of trainable quantities.
neurips-2023-memory-efficient-fine-tunin.tldr: PEQA fine-tunes compressed language models by updating only quantization scales, preserving low-bit structure while recovering strong performance.

paragraphs: Graph generators are often trained using the full adjacency matrix, which specifies the connections in each training graph. This paper studies training a deep generator from aggregate graph statistics instead. Traditional graph generators already use statistical matching, and learning from summaries has also been proposed as a way to protect privacy.

The authors develop an architecture that trains a deep graph generator to match statistics while preserving local differential privacy guarantees. This changes the information supplied during learning: the model learns from aggregate properties rather than the entire connection structure. The aim is to retain realistic graph generation while working within that privacy-preserving setting.

Across eight datasets, the deep model generates more realistic graphs than the traditional generators compared under the same statistics-only training condition. The authors also compare it with leading deep generators trained on full adjacency matrices. Their findings indicate that statistics are often enough to produce a competitive deep generator. That qualified result supports useful graph generation with local privacy, without claiming that summaries always replace full graph information.
neurips-2023-neural-graph-generation-fro.tldr: A deep graph generator trained on aggregate statistics produces competitive graphs while preserving local differential privacy guarantees.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness needs to extend beyond the examples used for training. This paper studies theoretical bounds on that robust generalization using network norms and a PAC-Bayesian approach. A central obstacle is controlling how changes to network weights affect behavior when adversarial perturbations are also involved.

The authors develop a spectrally normalized robust generalization bound that addresses this obstacle. They report that earlier approaches introduced strong extra assumptions and loose terms, whereas their bound avoids those additional assumptions and is substantially tighter. Its form aligns with standard generalization bounds, narrowing a gap that had appeared in prior theoretical analyses.

This alignment changes how the earlier mismatch should be interpreted. The authors attribute those extra mismatch terms to mathematical issues in the bounds, rather than treating them as explanations for poor robust generalization. The result concerns the analysis of generalization; it does not establish that robust and ordinary prediction have identical practical difficulty. The paper also extends its main result to attacks beyond general ℓp formulations and to other neural network architectures.
neurips-2023-pac-bayesian-spectrally-nor.tldr: A tighter PAC-Bayesian robust generalization bound removes extra assumptions and mismatch terms present in earlier analyses.

paragraphs: Multi-objective optimization seeks solutions that balance competing goals rather than minimize one number. This paper studies the minimum weight base problem, which abstracts problems such as multi-objective minimum spanning trees. Its focus is the runtime of MOEA/D, an evolutionary algorithm that decomposes multiple objectives into single-objective components.

The analysis first establishes properties of the convex hull of the nondominated front, including its approximation quality and a bound on its number of extreme points. These properties support a runtime guarantee: with an appropriate decomposition, MOEA/D finds all extreme points in expected fixed-parameter polynomial time in the oracle model. The guarantee is therefore tied to the decomposition setting and the stated computational model.

Experiments on random minimum spanning tree instances with two objectives agree with the theoretical findings. MOEA/D also finds all extreme points much faster than the compared GSEMO algorithm across the tested instances. The contribution connects the geometry of competing solutions to a rigorous explanation of when decomposition can make evolutionary search effective.
neurips-2023-rigorous-runtime-analysis-o.tldr: The paper proves a conditional runtime guarantee for MOEA/D to find all extreme points in multi-objective minimum weight base problems.

paragraphs: Suppose several experts each observe private information and report a probability for a binary event. A principal wants to combine those reports into an accurate forecast but does not know the joint distribution of the private information and outcomes. The available training examples contain expert reports and realized outcomes, rather than the experts’ underlying signals.

The paper asks how many independent examples are needed to learn an aggregator whose expected squared prediction error is within ε of optimal. For arbitrary discrete distributions, it proves a lower bound of approximately m^(n−2)/ε, suppressing logarithmic factors. Here n is the number of experts and m is each expert’s signal-space size. Thus, general aggregation can require exponentially more examples as the number of experts grows.

The picture changes if experts’ signals are independent conditional on the event outcome. Under that assumption, the authors give an upper bound of approximately 1/ε² that does not depend on n. A reduction from distribution learning explains the general difficulty, and the results also extend to nonbinary events.
neurips-2023-sample-complexity-of-foreca.tldr: Learning to aggregate forecasts can require exponentially many samples, but conditional independence yields a bound independent of the number of experts.

paragraphs: This paper studies agents that collectively optimize local objectives while each satisfying its own safety constraints. Objectives and constraints can be nonlinear functions of long-run state-action occupancy, allowing goals involving risk, exploration, or imitation. The challenge is that the joint state-action space grows exponentially with agent count, while safety constraints create dependencies across agents.

The proposed primal-dual method uses shadow rewards and restricts communication to neighbors within κ hops. This truncation relies on a correlation decay property that supports limiting the influence of more distant agents. The communication radius becomes a way to trade local computation and communication against approximation accuracy.

In the exact setting, the method converges to a first-order stationary point at rate O(T⁻²ᐟ³). With samples, it requires approximately ε⁻³⋅⁵ samples, up to logarithmic factors, to reach an ε-stationary point with high probability, alongside an approximation error O(φ₀²κ) for φ₀ between zero and one. Larger neighborhoods reduce that error term. Numerical experiments demonstrate effectiveness, while the theoretical target is stationarity rather than global optimality.
neurips-2023-scalable-primal-dual-actor-.tldr: A local-communication primal-dual method provides stationary-point guarantees for constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning under a correlation decay property.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the computational cost of training differentially private regression models on sparse inputs. Its starting point is that sparsity should help reduce training work, yet the authors identify a lack of methods designed to exploit it in this setting. Their contribution adapts Frank-Wolfe optimization to make effective use of sparse data.

Specifically, the abstract describes a sparse-aware adaptation of Frank-Wolfe for ℓ1-penalized linear regression. The stated training cost changes from O(TDS + TNS) to O(NS + T√D log D + TS²), where T is the iteration count, N is the number of rows, D is the feature count, and S describes sparsity. The new expression separates an NS term from the terms repeated over iterations.

This matters because the former bound repeatedly includes work proportional to both feature count and dataset size. The reported runtime reduction reaches up to 2,200 times, depending on sparsity and the privacy parameter ε. That figure is a best reported speedup under particular conditions, while the complexity expressions explain how the benefit depends on the problem’s dimensions.
neurips-2023-scaling-up-differentially-p.tldr: Sparse-aware Frank-Wolfe iterations reduce the training cost of differentially private regression, with reported speedups reaching 2,200 times.

paragraphs: With a fixed training-token budget, the choice of data can matter as much as its volume. This paper investigates whether language models learn interdependent skills in an order that can guide data selection. It defines skills and ordered skill sets through their associated data, making the idea concrete enough to study and use during training.

Experiments on synthetic and real data show ordered skill relationships in which training on prerequisites helps models acquire more advanced skills with less data. The authors use this framework to develop Skill-It, an online sampling algorithm over mixtures of skills. It supports learning multiple skills during continual pretraining and focusing on an individual target skill during fine-tuning.

On LEGO, Skill-It improves accuracy by 37.5 points over random sampling. On Natural Instructions, it reduces target-skill validation loss by 13.6% compared with training only on that skill’s data. A three-billion-parameter model continually pretrained on RedPajama achieves higher evaluation accuracy with one billion tokens than uniform source sampling achieves with three billion. These findings support selecting data through skill relationships.
neurips-2023-skill-it-a-data-driven-skil.tldr: Skill-It uses observed prerequisite relationships between skills to select training data more efficiently for language models.

paragraphs: In matching markets such as school choice, predictions can help participants decide which matches they prefer. Those preferences then feed into the mechanism that assigns matches. This paper examines the feedback between prediction and matching, arguing that analyzing the two mechanisms separately can miss an incentive to manipulate future outcomes.

The authors introduce an adversarial interaction attack. A participant that returns to the market, such as a school, can interact with its current matches in a way that sacrifices short-term performance but distorts future predictions. They build a formal economic model that captures how these interactions affect predictions, preference formation, and later matching decisions.

In a simplified setting, the authors prove that returning participants can benefit from this strategy. The gains increase as predictions become more accurate and more trusted. They also show that the attack increases inequality among students. The result identifies a specific vulnerability in the combined system: better predictive assistance can strengthen strategic incentives when the behavior generating future prediction data is itself controllable.
neurips-2023-strategic-behavior-in-two-s.tldr: A formal matching-market model shows how returning participants can sacrifice short-term performance to manipulate predictions and improve future matches.

paragraphs: This paper studies the algorithmic difficulty of finding globally optimal weights and biases for a fully connected neural network on a given dataset. The problem is empirical risk minimization: finding the best fit to those observations. The authors prove that this task is complete for the complexity class ∃R, connecting it to solving polynomial equations over real numbers.

The hardness already appears in networks with two inputs, two outputs, and one hidden layer of ReLU neurons. It therefore does not require a deep architecture or high-dimensional input. The authors also show that some instances require arbitrary algebraic numbers as optimal weights, even when every training data point has rational coordinates.

These results strengthen an earlier hardness result and have a conditional consequence for exact search. For networks with more than one output dimension, a combinatorial search algorithm of the cited kind cannot exist unless NP equals ∃R. The focus is exact optimal training: the theorem characterizes the mathematical complexity of that goal and the numerical forms optimal weights may require.
neurips-2023-training-fully-connected-ne.tldr: Exactly optimizing even small fully connected ReLU networks is ∃R-complete, and some rational datasets require algebraic optimal weights.

paragraphs: A segmentation model used in a surgical scene needs useful confidence estimates as well as accurate predictions. This paper addresses calibration: how well the model’s confidence corresponds to prediction risk. The authors argue that existing uncertainty methods lack explicit optimization guidance connecting those two quantities.

Their Fine-grained Reward Maximization framework turns a calibration metric into a reward and uses reinforcement learning to fine-tune a segmentation model pretrained through evidential learning. The update scheme also treats parameters differently. It weights their updates using parameter importance quantified by the Fisher information matrix, giving the reward a fine-grained role in adjusting the network.

Experiments cover two large surgical scene segmentation datasets and two uncertainty estimation settings. The method outperforms the compared leading approaches across all reported calibration metrics while maintaining high segmentation accuracy. At inference, it uses one forward pass and operates in real time. The results show improved calibration alongside practical prediction efficiency in the evaluated settings, addressing confidence quality without requiring repeated forward passes.
neurips-2023-uncertainty-estimation-for-.tldr: FGRM directly optimizes calibration rewards with parameter-specific updates to improve uncertainty estimates in surgical scene segmentation.

paragraphs: The paper studies how two opposing players can learn in zero-sum games using bandit feedback. It seeks an algorithm that is uncoupled, convergent, and rational, with finite-time guarantees for approaching Nash equilibrium. Uncoupled learning is central here: the method removes synchronization, prior-knowledge, and entropy-value communication requirements found in the compared approaches.

The analysis begins with stateless matrix games and establishes a last-iterate convergence rate of approximately t⁻¹ᐟ⁸, suppressing logarithmic factors. Last-iterate convergence concerns the current learned strategy rather than only an average over past strategies. For irreducible Markov games, the authors obtain a last-iterate rate of approximately t⁻¹ᐟ⁽⁹⁺ε⁾ for any positive ε.

Without assumptions on the game dynamics, the guarantee changes to a newly defined notion called path convergence, with rate approximately t⁻¹ᐟ¹⁰. Keeping these guarantees distinct matters because the unrestricted setting receives a different convergence result. The algorithm builds on entropy regularization while eliminating the need to communicate entropy values, supporting entirely uncoupled learning under the stated feedback model.
neurips-2023-uncoupled-and-convergent-le.tldr: An entirely uncoupled bandit-feedback algorithm provides finite convergence rates for zero-sum matrix and Markov games, with guarantees depending on the dynamics.
